hook: Keep an eye on the pronouns. The whole document is narrated by a voice that shouldn't be there, and once you work out why, the containment procedures read very differently. It's short enough to read twice, and the second pass is worth it.
whyItMatters:
426 turns an ordinary kitchen appliance into an anomaly purely through grammar: the effect is not something the report describes so much as something the report suffers from. That makes it a neat demonstration that an article's prose can itself be the anomalous property.

It is a very short entry, and almost every sentence pulls double duty as both documentation and evidence of the effect at work.
thingsToNotice:
The anomaly is a plain toaster that anyone describing it can only refer to in the first person, which is why the file opens with a cheerful hello. The comedy then runs straight into the discovery story, told in the same chirpy voice: the young wife died trying to eat an electric socket, her mother-in-law ate nearly 10 kg of bread until her stomach burst, the husband bled to death after a redacted attempt involving the toaster itself, and the grandfather was found starving, still waiting for toast to pop a week after loading bread. That is the long-exposure effect, people coming to believe they are toasters and hurting themselves trying to work like one.

The experiments are small and pointed. A D-class who knows nothing guesses a monster is locked in the cell and describes it in the first person without noticing; another, isolated with the toaster for 45 days, hugs it and calls it his brother; a single removed screw becomes 'my screw', so destroying the object would not end the effect. The closing note from the researcher thanks God for the effect's limits in a sentence whose pronouns have already gone wrong, which shows the joke has already reached the staff.
